newsitem.title: USA: Treasury Secretary defends U.S. China policy.
newsitem.headline: Treasury Secretary defends U.S. China policy.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Sunday defended President Bill Clinton's policy of engagement with China but said it could change if Beijing illegally sought to influence U.S. elections.

At hearings last week of a investigative panel, Republican and Democratic senators said it appeared that China tried last year to influence U.S. elections, but they disagreed on the extent of that attempt.
"I don't know the committee has concluded anything yet," Rubin said on NBC television's "Meet the Press."

"If ultimately conclusions are reached that improper actions have been taken, they will be viewed with great seriousness by the administration and reacted to appropropriately," he said, reiterating the White House's position.
The Senate panel probing campaign fund-raising scandals last week focused on John Huang, a former Democratic Party fund-raiser who worked in the Commerce Department from June 1994 to January 1996.

Republicans are trying to show that he handed over U.S. secrets to his former employer, the Indonesian-based conglomerate Lippo Group, which in turn could have passed them on to China. But they have only presented circumstantial evidence so far.

"That is what has not yet been shown -- that any Chinese money affected the presidental race in 1996," said Senator Carl Levin, a Democrat from Michigan, on Cable News Network's programme Late Edition. "In terms of drawing dots between China and the presidential race, those dots are not yet there."
However, some in Washington do see a link.

"There is no doubt in my mind, based on the evidence that I have seen, that there was an attempt by the Chinese government to influence congressional campaigns, state officials, and the presidential race," said Senator Susan Collins, a Republican from Maine, on the same programme.
Rubin repeated that the administration had not been influenced by foreign campaign contributions. Its "decisions, I can assure you, have been made on the merits and totally on the merits," he said.

"We have a policy of engagement, and I think it is a sensible policy both to pursue the nation's economic interest and also to pursue our very strong interests in nonproliferation and the rest," Rubin said.
